Native engine: paths and defined parameters

Source: vignettes/articles/model-native.qmd

Write the model as syntax and fit it by maximum likelihood with no other package. This is the first of five pages on the native engine. Part of the Models collection.

Structure any path model you can write as syntax; this page uses simple mediation
Class returned SEMFit, then MediationData from extract_mediation()
Routes fit_sem(syntax, data), or fit_mediation(model = syntax, engine = "native")
Syntax ?"medfit-syntax" lists every statement

The five pages: this one (paths and defined parameters), a latent mediator, constraints and the MBCO test, and several mediators and weights, and categorical covariates.

library(medfit)

Attaching package: 'medfit'
The following object is masked from 'package:stats':

    decompose
library(generics)

Attaching package: 'generics'
The following objects are masked from 'package:base':

    as.difftime, as.factor, as.ordered, intersect, is.element, setdiff,
    setequal, union

Fit it

Label a path with name * variable; := defines a new quantity from labels and gives it a delta-method standard error.

syntax <- "
  mediator1 ~ a * treatment + covariate1 + covariate2
  outcome ~ b * mediator1 + cp * treatment + covariate1 + covariate2
  ab := a * b
  total := cp + a * b
"
fit <- fit_sem(syntax, mediation_demo)
fit
SEMFit (native maximum likelihood)
==================================

  Observations:  400
  Parameters:    15 free, 0 df
  Information:   observed
  Std. errors:   model-based
  Converged:     Yes

Defined parameters:
  ab              0.3328  (SE 0.0642)
  total           0.5386  (SE 0.1187)

Use summary() for the parameter table and diagnostics.

fit_sem() returns a SEMFit. Read the defined parameters straight from it:

fit@defined
   name       expr       est         se
1    ab      a * b 0.3327695 0.06415544
2 total cp + a * b 0.5385678 0.11873128

summary(fit) prints the full parameter table and the optimizer diagnostics.

Get the usual objects

extract_mediation() turns the fit into a MediationData, so nie(), tidy() and the bootstrap work as on any other page:

x <- extract_mediation(fit, treatment = "treatment", mediator = "mediator1",
                       outcome = "outcome")
class(x)[1]
[1] "medfit::MediationData"
tidy(x, type = "effects", conf_int = TRUE)
# A tibble: 3 × 5
  term  estimate std_error conf_low conf_high
  <chr>    <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 nie      0.333    0.0642  0.207       0.459
2 nde      0.206    0.109  -0.00801     0.420
3 te       0.539    0.119   0.306       0.771

For one mediator, fit_mediation() does both steps:

x2 <- fit_mediation(model = syntax, data = mediation_demo,
                    treatment = "treatment", mediator = "mediator1",
                    engine = "native")
nie(x2)
Natural Indirect Effect (NIE): 0.3328

Intercepts

Writing any intercept (y ~ 1, or 1 as a term, y ~ 1 + x) turns the mean structure on and frees an intercept for every observed variable you did not mention, as lavaan does. The paths, variances and their standard errors are then the same as without it; the fit also reports the intercepts and the mean of each exogenous variable.

paths <- "mediator1 ~ a * treatment\noutcome ~ b * mediator1 + cp * treatment"
free <- fit_sem(paste0(paths, "\noutcome ~ 1"), mediation_demo)
tidy(free)[tidy(free)$op == "~1", c("term", "estimate", "std_error")]
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  term        estimate std_error
  <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>
1 outcome~1      0.231    0.0774
2 mediator1~1    0.155    0.0763
3 treatment~1    0.502    0.0250

An intercept you fix or constrain is a restriction, so it can change the other estimates. Fixing the outcome intercept at 0 costs one degree of freedom, and anova() compares the two fits:

zero <- fit_sem(paste0(paths, "\noutcome ~ 0*1"), mediation_demo)
c(free = free@theta[["cp"]], fixed_at_zero = zero@theta[["cp"]])
         free fixed_at_zero
   0.04057665    0.26236776 
anova(free, zero)
Likelihood-ratio (chi-square difference) test for SEMFit models

n = 400; Chisq is n times the minimized discrepancy

     Df  Chisq Chisq diff Df diff Pr(>Chisq)
free  0 0.0000
zero  1 8.8141     8.8141       1   0.002989 **
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Equating two intercepts works the same way (i1 == i2 with labels i1 and i2). meanstructure = TRUE turns the mean structure on without writing any intercept, and meanstructure = FALSE fits covariances only. A latent variable’s mean is fixed at 0, and a free latent intercept stops with “latent means are planned for a later release”. extract_mediation() reads the paths exactly as before; add a product term and it returns the four-way decomposition (below).

Compared with the glm engine

The two engines agree on the estimates and differ slightly in the standard errors, because the native engine uses maximum-likelihood (not least-squares) variances:

glm_fit <- fit_mediation(
  outcome ~ treatment + mediator1 + covariate1 + covariate2,
  mediator1 ~ treatment + covariate1 + covariate2,
  data = mediation_demo, treatment = "treatment", mediator = "mediator1"
)
rbind(native = tidy(x, type = "effects")$std_error,
      glm = tidy(glm_fit, type = "effects")$std_error)
             [,1]      [,2]      [,3]
native 0.06415544 0.1090891 0.1187313
glm    0.06449767 0.1097774 0.1194466

Product terms

x:m (the colon, no spaces) on the right side of a regression is the product of two observed variables, as in lavaan. The engine builds the column x * m from data after listwise deletion and treats it as an observed exogenous variable, so the likelihood, the constraints and the mean structure are the same as for any other regressor. x:m and m:x are one term, stored under the canonical name (the two names sorted in the C locale, m:x), and a label (b*x:m) names the coefficient. A product turns the mean structure on. Writing the treatment-by-mediator product in the outcome equation makes extract_mediation() return the four-way decomposition; the interaction page runs a worked example, including why centering the mediator matters.

four <- fit_sem(
  "mediator1 ~ treatment
   outcome_int ~ treatment + mediator1 + mediator1:treatment",
  mediation_demo, se_type = "sandwich"
)
Warning: the model test is not valid for this model: the product
'mediator1:treatment' has an endogenous factor ('mediator1'). `glance()` and
`summary()` report the chi-square, df and p-value as NA, and `anova()` and
`mbco_sem()` refuse. The coefficients equal equation-wise OLS, and the sandwich
standard errors (observed information) are unaffected.
tidy(four)[1:4, c("term", "estimate", "std_error")]
# A tibble: 4 × 3
  term                            estimate std_error
  <chr>                              <dbl>     <dbl>
1 mediator1~treatment               0.456     0.108
2 outcome_int~treatment             0.0405    0.119
3 outcome_int~mediator1             0.713     0.0699
4 outcome_int~mediator1:treatment   0.500     0.102

The warning above says the global model test is not available for this model, because the product contains the mediator, which is a regression target (details below). The coefficients and the sandwich standard errors are unaffected.

A product is fitted only in the class below. Anything else stops, naming the feature, with a message that says it is not yet supported with products; the same model works without the product. Each row gives the limit and the start of its message.

Limit Message (starts with, or contains)
A space around : “a product ‘:’ needs a variable name on each side, written without spaces (x:m)”
x:x, x:m:w “of a variable with itself is not supported”, “a three-way or higher product”
A product as a left side (x:m ~ y, x:m ~~ y) “cannot be a left side”
A product in =~ or in a constraint expression “is only valid on the right side of a regression”
A latent variable in a product “products with latent variables are not supported in this version”
One product twice in an equation “are the same product (canonical name”
A factor that is the target or downstream of it (y ~ x + x:y) “(rule 8: no outcome-derived regressors)”
A loop of regressions “The model is not recursive”
A residual covariance between outcomes “A product model cannot have a residual covariance (rule 9)”
A label shared by two rows “is used on more than one parameter”
A fixed coefficient “has a fixed coefficient (rule 9)”
An inline bound on a coefficient or intercept (lower(0)*x) “has a bound (rule 9”
==, < or > naming a coefficient label (a < 1 too) “names the coefficient label”
A fixed, shared or constrained intercept “(rule 9, intercept clause”
meanstructure = FALSE “meanstructure = FALSE, but the model has a product term”
A data column m:x that is not x * m “is not the product of”
A product input that is not numeric, factor, character or logical (a date) “needs numeric variables”
information = "expected", endogenous factor “is not available for a model with a product of an endogenous variable”
anova() or mbco_sem(), endogenous factor “is not available for” … “a model with a product term”
extract_mediation() with another product on the treatment or mediator “the native extraction does not support the product”

Two more facts are not errors. The covariance that completion would add between two pure outcomes is fixed at 0 in a product model, with one note; and fit_sem() warns once when a product is fitted without se_type = "sandwich", which is the standard-error choice because a product is not normal. fixed_x = TRUE fixes the product columns with the other exogenous variables.

The global chi-square is not valid when a factor of the product is itself a regression target (the model treats the product as exogenous although it is a function of that variable), or when the exogenous (co)variance block is restricted. glance() then reports chi-square, df and p-value as NA with a note, and anova() and mbco_sem() refuse. A product of exogenous variables with a free block keeps the ordinary test. Methods and Formulas gives the reason.

Limits

  • Observed means only. A free latent mean or intercept stops with “latent means are planned for a later release”; the latent variable’s mean is fixed at 0 (see Intercepts).
  • Constraints on an intercept are checked up to a data mean about 1,000 times the standard deviation; beyond that the fit may stop with “no start converged”. Constraints that leave every intercept free have no such limit.
  • A label must be defined before := can use it; an unknown label stops with “unknown parameter label”.
  • Exogenous variables get free variances and covariances, as lavaan does with fixed.x = FALSE, so they appear in the parameter table. fixed_x = TRUE (or a vector of names) fixes the selected ones at the sample moments, as fixed.x = TRUE does: the structural estimates, their standard errors and the degrees of freedom do not change, the parameter count falls, and logLik(), AIC and BIC become conditional on the fixed variables, so fits with different fixed sets cannot be compared.
  • AIC and BIC across product and no-product fits are not comparable. The product column is an extra observed variable in the joint likelihood, so a fit with x:m and the same model without it describe different data (on mediation_demo, the same outcome gives AIC 3934.7 with the product and 2994.1 without). AIC(fit_a, fit_b), BIC(fit_a, fit_b), anova() and mbco_sem() refuse such a pair, naming the observed variables that differ.
  • Products are limited to two observed variables inside the class in the table above; latent products, x:x and three-way products stop with the messages listed there.
  • Factor covariates (a factor, character or logical column on a regression’s right side) become 0/1 dummies named g_b, g_c (reference: the first level), as lm() builds them. A label on the factor (b*g) stops; label one dummy (b*g_b). A factor as an outcome, a mediator or a four-way treatment is not supported, and g:m expands to one product per dummy (see ?"medfit-syntax").
  • summary() reports diagnostics, including an improper solution and any active bound or constraint; read them before trusting a fit.

Stability

The exported signatures of fit_sem() and mbco_sem(), the SEMFit properties and the model syntax in ?"medfit-syntax" change only through a deprecation. New syntax and new properties can be added: a name, a table row or a property that exists today keeps its meaning. This matters for the features listed under Limits (a categorical mediator or outcome, for example): they will arrive as additions, not as a rename of g_b-style dummy names or of the m:x product name. A test (test-api-freeze.R) pins the current names. Numerical fixes are not breaking changes.
